title: The Man Who Walked to the River
subtitle: Balarama Refuses to Take Sides and Departs for the Saraswati Tirthas
story:
Of all the warriors who stood on the field of Kurukshetra that day, one of the greatest was taking no part in the war — and he was Krishna's own elder brother. The Pandava camp had given the order to draw up for battle, and across the field the Kaurava host was arming to meet it: two branches of one royal family, the five sons of Pandu and the hundred sons of the blind king Dhritarashtra, come at last to fight over a kingdom they could not share. In the middle of that vast gathering of kings and soldiers, Balarama, a mighty warrior of the Vrishni clan, stood apart and would not arm.

He would not fight against the Pandavas, and he would not fight against Duryodhana. Both armies held men he had known all his life, and he would raise his arm against neither. Yet his refusal was not a turning away from the quarrel. "As for me," he said, "I cannot bear to face the world without Krishna on my side. Whatever Krishna sets out to achieve, I follow."

So he followed Krishna's cause without holding anything back — but following it was not the same as standing on the field to watch it carried out. "I am going to the fords of the Saraswati to bathe," he said, "for I cannot look on unmoved while the Kauravas are destroyed." The Kauravas were his kin, and so were the Pandavas; the only way to be true to both was to stand with neither.

So, while the kings armed themselves and the soldiers raised their joyful uproar and the two hosts settled into their places, Balarama turned his back on the field. The camp behind him rang with the noise of preparation — hammers on chariots, the shouts of captains, the stamping of war-elephants — and he walked the other way, toward stillness. The road before him ran away from the tents and banners, down toward the Saraswati, the sacred river of the sages, whose fords, the tirthas, were holy bathing places where pilgrims had come for ages to wash and pray. There he would bathe, and there he would wait out the war. His refusal was no judgment that one army was right and the other wrong. It was simply the position left to a man who loved both sides and could not bear to see one of them destroyed.

The greatest war of the age would be fought without him, and the two brothers of the Vrishni house parted at its edge — Krishna to ride into the battle at his friend's side, Balarama to the quiet water. Behind him the dust of the camps rose and the armies finished arranging themselves; ahead, the Saraswati ran between its banks, asking nothing of any man.
reflection: Balarama's withdrawal is not indifference: he follows Krishna's cause with his whole heart and still cannot stand on the field to watch it carried out. Devotion and kinship pull him in different directions, and the honest answer to an unbearable war turns out to be a long walk to the river — letting the water carry what the field cannot.
next_story_tease: On the morning of battle, Krishna would bid Arjuna hymn Durga for victory.
hero_scene: At the edge of the Pandava camp, Balarama walks away from the field with his back to the drawn-up armies, his staff in hand, the river Saraswati glittering ahead of him while banners and dust rise behind.
